text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS

SAFETY WARNING — READ FIRST: A burning smell near the steering column combined with flashing ABS and airbag (SRS) lamps is a stop-driving condition. The steering column houses the clockspring, the airbag squib wiring, and in many Transit builds a portion of the restraint control module (RCM) harness runs directly behind the lower column shroud. Any heat signature in that area, even faint, must be treated as a potential wiring fire risk until a technician confirms otherwise. Do not continue shuttle operation until this is inspected.

- Root cause (working theory): the aftermarket dash camera's hardwire kit was tapped into the fuse panel and routed near the steering column area. Repeated bump/flex loading from shuttle-run duty cycles has likely caused the added wire (or the factory harness it was spliced into or zip-tied against) to chafe, pinch, or intermittently short to ground/chassis. This produces a momentary voltage disturbance on a shared circuit that feeds both the HS-CAN backbone and restraint-related wiring, which lines up with both reported codes.
- U0100 (Lost Communication With ECM/PCM) is a standard OBD-II network code. It does not mean the PCM failed — it means another module, or the gateway itself, briefly stopped hearing PCM messages on the High-Speed CAN bus. This is classic symptomology for an intermittent short, a chafed harness, or a voltage drop severe enough to reset a module mid-cycle — which is exactly what a bump-triggered short would produce.
- B1234 is a Ford enhanced body code, not a generic SAE code, so its exact text varies by module and firmware. Based on the pattern presented (airbag lamp flash, steering column heat, bump correlation), the most probable definition is a restraint system circuit continuity or resistance fault tied to the steering column wiring path (commonly associated with clockspring or column-harness circuits on Transit-based RCM strategies). This must be confirmed with Ford's IDS/FDRS scan tool pulling the full code description and any associated Pending/Continuous Memory Codes — a generic reader will not give you the true definition.
- Component failure analysis: this is not a "normal wear" failure pattern for a 2021 Transit at this stage of its service life. The trigger event (installation of an aftermarket accessory tapped into the fuse panel) plus the trigger condition (bumps) is a textbook wiring-integrity issue, not a module or sensor degradation issue. Ground faults introduced by improperly routed or improperly grounded aftermarket wiring are one of the top causes of intermittent multi-module CAN faults in fleet vehicles with add-on electronics.
- Age/mileage considerations: mileage was not provided, but this failure signature is independent of mileage — it is installation-and-vibration dependent. A vehicle with low mileage but heavy shuttle-route bump exposure can develop this fault faster than a high-mileage vehicle driven gently, because the chafe point is mechanically driven, not wear-driven.
- Confidence: 72%. This is a strong circumstantial match, but I cannot confirm the exact B1234 definition, the exact tap location of the dash cam, or whether the clockspring itself has already been damaged without a live scan and a physical harness inspection.

Data Needed:
- Full FDRS/IDS scan printout showing the exact B1234 text, module of origin, and Continuous Memory Codes with freeze-frame data.
- Photos of the dash camera's hardwire tap point at the fuse panel and its full routing path toward the steering column.
- A wiggle test video/notes: does the ABS/airbag lamp flash reproduce when the dash cam wiring or steering column trim is flexed by hand?
- Voltage drop reading across the tapped fuse circuit under load, and the amperage rating of the fuse/fuse-tap used for the camera.
- Confirmation of whether the steering column has been removed/serviced previously (aftermarket install disturbance to the clockspring connector is common).

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

- Aftermarket wiring short/chafe at the dash cam tap (high likelihood): matches the bump-triggered timing, the burning smell location, and the dual-code pattern (network dropout plus restraint circuit code) far better than any single internal component failure would.
- Clockspring degradation (medium likelihood): steering column clocksprings can develop internal wire fatigue from steering input over time, which sets airbag-related codes and can bleed into CAN reporting if the column connector shares a splice pack with other harnesses. This is elevated on the differential specifically because the smell and lamp behavior are column-centric, but it does not naturally explain a fuse-panel-tied U0100 unless the dash cam tap disturbed that same connector during install.
- Fuse panel connector/pin corrosion or a loose spade terminal from the aftermarket "add-a-fuse" tap (medium likelihood): a poorly seated tap can create resistance heating exactly at the fuse panel, which is often physically close to the steering column area on Transit dash construction, and can explain both the smell and intermittent module resets.
- Restraint Control Module internal fault (low likelihood): RCM hardware failures are uncommon at this stage and typically set a steady code, not one that correlates tightly with road bumps and an aftermarket accessory install timeline.
- PCM/BCM internal fault (low likelihood): U0100 with no other powertrain drivability complaints and a very specific mechanical trigger (bumps) argues strongly against an internal control module defect.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION

- Full visual/physical inspection of the dash cam wiring from the windshield mount down through the A-pillar to the fuse panel tap and steering column area, checking for melted insulation, discoloration, or a pinched wire against the column bracket. No special tool required; approximately 0.5 hour, $60–90.
- Ford IDS or FDRS full vehicle network scan pulling every module's DTCs, not just the flagged codes, plus the exact B1234 definition and any U-code companion faults (U0101, U0121, U0140 are common companions when a shared harness is involved). Expect $130–180 for a dedicated network diagnostic hour.
- Live wiggle test with the scan tool connected in "all-DTC monitor" mode while a second technician flexes the dash cam wiring and the steering column lower shroud — if the ABS/airbag lamps flash or U0100/B1234 re-trigger during the flex, the fault location is confirmed. Roughly 0.5–1.0 hour, $75–150.
- Voltage drop test across the aftermarket fuse tap under key-on/engine-running load using a digital multimeter; a drop over roughly 0.2V on a properly rated circuit indicates a bad tap or overloaded circuit. About 15 minutes, typically bundled into the diagnostic hour at no extra charge.
- Amperage/fuse-rating check: confirm the dash cam kit did not tap a circuit already near capacity, and that the tap uses a proper mini/mini-low-profile add-a-fuse rated for the original fuse's amperage, not a higher-rated substitute.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION

- "Can you show me the exact FDRS description for B1234, not just the code number?" — a shop that cannot produce the full text is guessing, not diagnosing.
- "Did you physically trace the dash cam wiring from the fuse panel to the steering column before quoting anything?" — if they went straight to a module or harness replacement quote without inspecting the aftermarket wiring, that is a major red flag given the install-and-bump correlation.
- "Did the fault reproduce during a wiggle test, and can I see that on video or in your notes?" — reproducibility is the standard for intermittent electrical work; "it didn't act up on the lift" without a bump/flex test is not an acceptable answer.
- "Are you recommending clockspring or RCM replacement based on a confirmed internal fault, or because the code is restraint-related?" — codes pointing at a system do not always mean that system's component is bad; wiring faults upstream are common.
- "Will removing or properly re-routing the aftermarket dash cam wiring be tested BEFORE any Ford part is replaced?" — if the answer is no, they are skipping the cheapest and most likely fix.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING

- Opening: "I've done some research on what U0100 and airbag-lamp flashing after bumps usually points to on a Transit with an aftermarket dash cam installed, and I want to understand your testing before we move forward."
- Phrasing: "I'm curious how you ruled the dash cam wiring in or out, since the burning smell is right where it was tapped in."
- Example dialogue: "Could you walk me through the wiggle test results? I'd like to see whether the fault reproduced when the column trim or camera wiring was flexed."
- Body language: stay calm, take notes on a clipboard or phone, ask to see the scan tool screen directly rather than a verbal summary — this signals you expect documentation without sounding accusatory.
- Response handling: if they get defensive, say "I'm not questioning your ability — I just want to authorize the right repair the first time, especially with airbag and ABS involved."
- Exit strategy: "I'd like a written, line-item diagnostic summary emailed to me before I approve any parts, given this involves my safety systems."
- Never say: "My AI report says..." or "I got a second opinion online." Always say: "I've done some research and want to understand..."

6. COST BREAKDOWN

- Dash cam wiring correction (removal of improper tap, re-routing away from the column, proper fused accessory tap or relay kit installed): typically 1.0–1.5 labor hours at $130–175/hr, $130–260, plus $15–40 in proper tap/fuse hardware.
- Diagnostic time (network scan plus wiggle test): $150–250 as outlined above; this should be credited toward the repair if the shop performs the fix, which is standard practice.
- If the clockspring is confirmed damaged (only after wiring is ruled in or out): OEM clockspring assembly typically runs $150–320 depending on trim/steering wheel controls, plus 1.0–1.8 labor hours ($130–315) for column disassembly, airbag system depower/repower, and a mandatory post-repair SRS system verification scan.
- Fair total range if it is wiring-only: $280–470. Fair total range if clockspring replacement is required: $460–850. Any quote significantly above this without a confirmed wiggle-test result or clockspring failure documentation should be questioned.
- Overcharge markers: RCM or PCM replacement quoted before a wiring inspection (+$400–900 unjustified), "diagnostic package" fees stacked with no printed findings, or steering column disassembly billed before the dash cam wiring has even been inspected.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION

- Parts cannon: quoting a clockspring, RCM, or BCM replacement without first performing the wiggle test on the aftermarket wiring is replacing expensive safety components to "see if it fixes it" at your expense.
- Diagnostic shortcut: reading the codes, seeing "airbag" and "ABS" in the description, and jumping straight to a restraint-system parts quote without pulling the full FDRS code text or testing the obvious aftermarket install first.
- Price gouging red flags: separate "electrical diagnostic," "network diagnostic," and "SRS diagnostic" fees all billed for what should be one connected diagnostic session; quoting steering column removal labor before confirming the fault is even in the column.
- Refusal to inspect the dash cam installation at all, treating it as "not our problem" — since the smell and code pattern began after that install and are triggered by bumps, it is the first and cheapest thing to rule in or out.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE

- Approve immediately: the combined network scan, full B1234 code pull, and physical wiggle-test inspection of the dash cam wiring and steering column harness. This is inexpensive and directly targets the most probable cause.
- Approve conditionally: any dash cam rewiring/relay-kit correction once the wiggle test confirms the aftermarket wiring as the fault source.
- Reject outright: RCM, PCM, or clockspring replacement quoted before a documented wiggle-test result is shown to you in writing or on video.
- Get a second opinion: if the shop cannot produce the full FDRS code description for B1234, or refuses to test the aftermarket wiring before recommending Ford-part replacement, take the vehicle to a shop or dealer with proper Ford diagnostic equipment.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION

- System operation: the Transit's modules (PCM, ABS module, RCM, BCM, instrument cluster) communicate over a High-Speed CAN bus. Each module reports its own status and listens for others; if one module's power, ground, or bus wiring is disturbed, other modules can briefly stop "hearing" it and log a U-code, even though the module itself is fine.
- Failure mechanism: aftermarket hardwire kits tapped into fuse panels introduce a new physical connection point and often route wire bundles through tight areas like the steering column shroud. Vibration and bump flex over thousands of shuttle-route cycles can wear insulation at a pinch point, creating an intermittent short to ground or a resistance point that heats up — producing the smell you noticed and disturbing shared circuits enough to set both a network code and a restraint-related code.
- Prevention: any aftermarket electrical accessory should be tapped using a proper fused add-a-circuit at a location away from tilt/telescope steering movement, secured with strain relief every few inches, and routed away from the column and pedal box. After installation, a wiggle test of the new wiring should be part of the install checklist, and the vehicle should be rescanned for stored codes before it re-enters service.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY

- If the wiring is the cause, no Ford part is needed — only proper wiring supplies (OEM-style fused tap connectors and heat-shrink butt splices) rated to the Transit's fuse panel amperage.
- If the clockspring is confirmed damaged, request the OEM clockspring assembly by VIN from a Ford dealer parts counter — Transit clockspring part numbers vary by steering wheel option (cruise/audio controls), so do not accept a generic aftermarket clockspring; a mismatched connector count can itself set additional restraint codes.
- Why OEM matters here specifically: the clockspring carries the airbag squib circuit; a non-OEM or improperly indexed replacement can produce a false "airbag ready" state, which is a life-safety risk in a shuttle vehicle carrying passengers.
- Pricing sources: get the exact part number and dealer price quote by VIN, then cross-check pricing at a second Ford dealer parts counter or a reputable OEM parts distributor before authorizing — clockspring pricing can vary $100+ between dealers for the identical part number.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS

- Ask for the diagnostic hour to be itemized and credited toward the repair if performed at the same shop — this is standard and reasonable to request up front.
- Ask directly: "If the wiggle test confirms the dash cam wiring, will the repair cost be limited to the rewire, or is there a minimum labor charge regardless of cause?"
- Get the OEM clockspring part number (if applicable) and call a second Ford dealer for a matching quote before authorizing column disassembly labor.
